outline: A progressive wave transfers energy as neighbouring particles vibrate about equilibrium. Describe displacement, amplitude, phase difference, period, frequency, wavelength and speed precisely. A CRO time-base gives time per division; y-gain gives voltage per division. In one period a wave advances one wavelength, so $v=f\lambda$. Intensity is power per area and is proportional to amplitude squared for waves of the same type in the same medium.

misconceptions.refutation: Amplitude is maximum displacement from equilibrium; peak-to-peak is twice it.

misconceptions.statement: CRO trace height directly gives sound displacement.
misconceptions.refutation: Y-gain converts screen height to voltage; microphone calibration is needed to obtain sound displacement.
misconceptions.contrast: screen amplitude in V versus particle amplitude in m

misconceptions.statement: One wavelength travels in one second.
misconceptions.refutation: One wavelength travels in one period, which is $1/f$.
At fixed medium and frequency, intensity is proportional to amplitude squared.
misconceptions.contrast: double amplitude gives four times intensity

misconceptions.statement: The medium travels with the wave.
misconceptions.refutation: Particles oscillate about equilibrium while the disturbance transfers energy.

items.examiner: The first loud sound corresponds to the first-order stationary sound wave in the cylinder, with a displacement node at the surface of the water and a displacement antinode at the open end of the cylinder. The second loud sound corresponds to the second-order stationary sound wave, again with a node at the surface of the water and an antinode at the open end of the cylinder, with one other node between the two. The change in the water level is the distance between two nodes, λ / 2. From this the wavelength and frequency of the sound can be calculated.

A cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO) is connected to a microphone which detects sound of constant
frequency.
The trace on the screen of the CRO is shown.
Which property of the sound wave is measured using only information from the CRO?
items.examiner: The amplitude of a sound wave is the maximum displacement from the equilibrium position, so its unit is m. The y-gain scale of the CRO is in units of V div–1. Using the amplitude of the CRO trace to determine the amplitude of the sound wave involves a calculation converting V to m, and this would require knowledge of the behaviour of the microphone. The time-base scale of the CRO is in units of s (or some multiple), so a direct reading of a single wave cycle on the horizontal axis of the CRO display would give the period of the wave.

flashcards.back: Propagation of a disturbance that transfers energy while particles vibrate about equilibrium.

flashcards.front: Define displacement, amplitude, period, frequency and wavelength.
flashcards.back: Displacement: position from equilibrium with direction. Amplitude: maximum displacement from equilibrium. Period: time for one complete oscillation. Frequency: oscillations per unit time. Wavelength: distance between successive points in phase.

flashcards.front: What are phase difference and wave speed?
flashcards.back: Phase difference: angular separation of oscillations. Wave speed: distance travelled by a wavefront per unit time.

9702-7.1.1.motivate: A ripple crosses a tank while a floating marker mostly bobs in place. What is actually travelling?
9702-7.1.1.establish: Wave motion is the propagation of a disturbance. In a rope, a pulse moves along while rope elements vibrate about equilibrium. In a spring, coils oscillate while the disturbance travels along the spring. In a ripple tank, the surface pattern spreads while water particles oscillate about equilibrium. The travelling disturbance transfers energy.
9702-7.1.1.connect: The distinction between the travelling pattern and local vibration prepares you to describe wave terms.
9702-7.1.1.note:
- Wave motion is propagation of a disturbance.
- Ropes, springs and ripple tanks show local vibration and travelling energy.
9702-7.1.1.self_explain: Describe what a rope element does after a pulse reaches it.

9702-7.1.2.motivate: A wave graph has heights and horizontal spacings. Each measurement answers a different question.
9702-7.1.2.establish: Displacement is a particle's distance and direction from equilibrium. Amplitude is maximum displacement from equilibrium. Period is time for one complete oscillation; frequency is the number of oscillations per unit time, $f=1/T$. Wavelength is the distance between successive points in phase. Phase difference is the angular separation of oscillations, with a full cycle equal to $360^\circ$ or $2\pi$ rad. Wave speed is distance travelled by a wavefront per unit time.
9702-7.1.2.connect: Use period and wavelength together to derive wave speed.
9702-7.1.2.note:
- Amplitude is measured from equilibrium to a peak.
- Period is one cycle; frequency is cycles per unit time.
- Wavelength joins consecutive points in phase.
9702-7.1.2.self_explain: How do period and wavelength differ on time and distance graphs?

9702-7.1.3.motivate: A CRO turns a changing electrical signal into a trace that can be measured.
9702-7.1.3.establish: The time-base gives time per horizontal division. Measure the width of one complete cycle, multiply by the time-base to find period $T$, then use $f=1/T$. The y-gain gives voltage per vertical division. Measure centre line to peak and multiply by y-gain for voltage amplitude. With a microphone, that voltage is not automatically the displacement amplitude of the air particles: microphone calibration is required to convert volts to metres.
9702-7.1.3.connect: The CRO supplies the frequency used in $v=f\lambda$.
9702-7.1.3.note:
- Time-base: time per horizontal division.
- Y-gain: voltage per vertical division.
- Use microphone calibration for sound-particle displacement.
9702-7.1.3.self_explain: Why is one peak-to-trough distance insufficient for the period?

9702-7.1.4.motivate: A wave moves exactly one wavelength during one period.
9702-7.1.4.establish: By the definition of speed, distance divided by time, $v=\lambda/T$ because a wavefront advances one wavelength in one period. Frequency is the number of cycles per unit time, so $f=1/T$. Substitute to derive $v=f\lambda$. The units check: Hz is $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and wavelength is m, yielding $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
9702-7.1.4.connect: The derived equation can now be rearranged to find any one of speed, frequency or wavelength.
9702-7.1.4.note:
- One wavelength advances in one period.
- $v=\lambda/T$ and $f=1/T$.
- Hence $v=f\lambda$.
9702-7.1.4.self_explain: Show the two equations needed to derive $v=f\lambda$.

9702-7.1.5.motivate: Frequency and wavelength change together when a wave enters a new situation.
9702-7.1.5.establish: Recall and use $v=f\lambda$. For speed, multiply frequency by wavelength. For frequency, use $f=v/\lambda$. For wavelength, use $\lambda=v/f$. Convert lengths to metres and time to seconds. At fixed speed, frequency and wavelength are inversely proportional: doubling frequency halves wavelength. State speed in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, frequency in Hz and wavelength in m.
9702-7.1.5.connect: This relation is also used with CRO frequency measurements and with intensity questions that mention changing wave conditions.
9702-7.1.5.note:
- $v=f\lambda$.
- Rearrange before substituting values.
- Convert units before calculating.
9702-7.1.5.self_explain: At fixed speed, what happens to wavelength when frequency triples?

9702-7.1.6.motivate: A wave can deliver energy to a distant point even though each particle moves only locally.
9702-7.1.6.establish: A progressive wave transfers energy in its direction of propagation. A disturbed rope element influences the next element; a ripple's disturbance passes across water. Each medium particle vibrates about equilibrium, so the transfer of energy does not require bulk transport of the medium. Distinguish the direction of propagation from the direction in which an individual particle moves.
9702-7.1.6.connect: Power measures energy transferred per unit time; intensity describes how this power is spread across an area.
9702-7.1.6.note:
- Progressive waves transfer energy.
- Medium particles vibrate about equilibrium.
- Propagation and particle motion are distinct.
9702-7.1.6.self_explain: Why can a cork bob in place while ripple energy moves away?

9702-7.1.7.motivate: The same wave power spread across a larger area gives a weaker wave at each square metre.
9702-7.1.7.establish: Intensity is the power transferred per unit area normal to the wave's direction, $I=P/A$, with unit $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. For comparable progressive waves in the same medium at the same frequency, intensity is proportional to the square of amplitude: $I\propto a^2$. Therefore $I_2/I_1=(a_2/a_1)^2$. Doubling amplitude gives four times the intensity; halving intensity makes amplitude $1/\sqrt{2}$ of its original value.
9702-7.1.7.connect: This connects energy transfer by a progressive wave to the measurable size of its vibration.
9702-7.1.7.note:
- Intensity is power per unit area: $I=P/A$.
- For comparable waves, $I\propto a^2$.
- Square the amplitude ratio to find intensity ratio.
9702-7.1.7.self_explain: What happens to intensity when amplitude triples?
